overview.text: Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL), also called Kirchhoff’s second law or the loop rule, says that the signed voltage changes encountered while tracing a closed circuit path add to zero: ΣΔV = 0. A rise and a drop take opposite signs; the sign assigned to each depends on the chosen travel direction and component polarity. In ordinary circuit analysis, this expresses that the energy supplied per unit charge balances the energy transferred to components around the loop. KVL helps turn circuit diagrams into equations for unknown voltages and currents, including in networks too complex for simple series-and-parallel reduction. It differs from Kirchhoff’s current law, which concerns currents at nodes. The standard form assumes no changing magnetic flux links the loop; otherwise, induction must be considered.

key_facts.text: KVL is also known as Kirchhoff’s second law or the loop rule.
Its equation is the algebraic sum of voltage changes around a closed loop equals zero: ΣΔV = 0.

Signs depend on the direction you trace the loop: for example, crossing a source from its negative to positive terminal counts as a rise, while crossing a resistor in the direction of current counts as a drop.
Applying KVL produces equations that can help solve for unknown circuit voltages and currents, including in more complex networks.
The usual loop-sum form applies when no time-varying magnetic flux links the loop; a changing flux requires accounting for electromagnetic induction.
